extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political economy, social reformers, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative analysis of the causes and mechanisms by which modern civilization advances or declines, emphasizing the roles of association, equality, land ownership, and the concentration of power. The chapter identifies signs of decline and suggests that public control of land rent would avert retrogression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for social progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress goes on just as society tends toward closer association and greater equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union and liberty are its factors: extension of commerce and exchanges, growth of international and municipal law, advances in security of property and person, individual liberty, and toward democratic government. These free the mental power that produces scientific discovery, inventions, and increased productive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to inequality with integration and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: As integration and specialization of functions increase in society, there is a constant liability to inequality unless social adjustments change to secure equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'garment' of laws and customs tends to become too tight as society develops; specialization and growth produce collective power distinguishable from individual powers, and unless redistributed this collective power lodges with a portion of the community and increases inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of collective power causes petrifaction
rubrics_metrics.description: When collective power is lodged in the hands of a portion of the community it tends to increase and to produce greater inequality, which checks and may halt improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include the patriarchal head becoming hereditary monarchy, military specialization concentrating power in chiefs, and religious, judicial, and administrative functions passing to special classes who magnify their function and extend their power. Resulting effects: waste of mental power, ostentation, luxury, warfare, and resistance to useful innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land ownership as the great cause of inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural monopoly created by possession of land is the great cause of inequality; private appropriation of land and rent strips producers of wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally land may have been treated as common property, but as population grows and rent arises, private appropriation concentrates ownership. Appropriation occurs by conquest, by dominant classes seizing public domain/common lands, and by political/religious classes acquiring land—leading to concentration and intensified inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism and habit impede improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of habit and possibility of mental/moral deterioration cause societies to cling to obsolete customs, laws, and institutions and permit growth of institutions that resist normal perceptions of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileged classes and close organizations (religion, law, medicine, trade guilds) instinctively dislike innovation and guard special knowledge/skill; this conservatism wastes the collective mental power freed by association and checks improvements that would relieve toil and increase power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery prevents progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery necessarily involves a waste of human power and cannot aid improvement; slave-holding peoples are not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slave labor is less productive than free labor; masters' power is wasted in holding slaves; slavery stifles invention and forbids utilization of discoveries. Historical claim: classical world’s slavery explains lack of great modern inventions despite polished literature and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political equality alone insufficient to prevent economic inequality's harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute political and legal equality does not by itself prevent the tendency to inequality caused by private land ownership; political equality coexisting with unequal wealth tends toward despotism or anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican forms can be hollowed out—despotism may grow in the name of the people if wealth is concentrated. Examples: Roman transition to autocracy despite forms, modern risks where money and corrupting interests buy power; political equality without economic equality can produce worse despotism or chaotic uprisings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic indicators of societal decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain economic trends signal that progress is reversing: wages and interest tend to fall, rent to rise, the rich become much richer, the poor more helpless, and the middle class is swept away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These trends indicate increasing inequality and the undermining of conditions for association and equality; they presage political degradation and social petrifaction if not checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of political decline and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that popular government is deteriorating include degraded legislative bodies, decline in standards of public life, increasing influence of money, reckless voting, shrinking ability to carry reforms, parties becoming controlled by oligarchies or dictatorships, and loss of principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete modern example: urban political machines where 'bosses' control nominations and offices, allowing corporations and pecuniary interests to pack legislatures and courts. These are symptoms that political institutions no longer protect equality or public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of wealth inequality on democratic government
rubrics_metrics.description: Where distribution of wealth is grossly unequal, increased democracy tends to worsen outcomes rather than improve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a few are so rich and many so poor that votes may be bought or sold, or the poor follow demagogues, democracy becomes vulnerable to jobbers and corrupt leaders; rotten democracy corrupts national character and may produce irreversible decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association promotes progress; war and slavery oppose it
rubrics_metrics.description: Association (co-operation, closer social ties) is the condition of civilization; war and slavery, being opposed to association, impede or reverse progress except in limited cases where war breaks anti-social barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War can only aid progress when it prevents further war or breaks down anti-social barriers; slavery is always a hindrance and has never been a genuine motor of civilization according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as the condition for invention and utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom—equality and liberty—is the stimulus and condition for progress and invention; leisure alone (as under slavery) does not produce invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: free labor fosters invention and utilization of discoveries; slave societies could be polished culturally but not inventive; freedom summons the mental power that harnesses nature and increases productive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous societies are more prone to petrifaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilizations arising from a homogeneous people developing under the same conditions tend to concentrate power and petrify more readily than civilizations formed from mixed, diverse communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Nile Valley and other homogeneous early civilizations built rigid caste and hereditary structures that blocked further progress; contrast with societies (e.g., Greece, Rome, later Europe) where diversity hindered total concentration and allowed more dynamic change—though Rome still decayed when inequality concentrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public control of land rent as remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Making land common property (or otherwise capturing land rent for public purposes) would remove the central cause of inequality and give an enormous impetus to civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter asserts this policy would prevent the unequal appropriation of rent that strips producers and concentrates power; it is presented as the practical corrective to the tendencies described, referenced to earlier proposal in the book.
